title: Pagination: OFFSET vs keyset
summary: Why `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` gets slower on deep pages and drifts when rows are inserted or deleted, and how keyset (seek) pagination fixes both: a total order with a unique tie-breaker, the `(created_at, id) < (x, y)` row comparison and its OR form, the composite index that serves it, previous pages, opaque API cursors, filters, `has_more` without counting, and when OFFSET is still fine.
prerequisiteNotes: sql-indexes: how a B-tree index stores rows in key order, what a composite index can serve (leading columns, sort direction) and how to read `EXPLAIN`. Keyset pagination is an index range scan, so you need to see why the column order of the index matters.
objectives: Explain why `OFFSET` cost grows with page depth and how inserts and deletes between requests duplicate or skip rows.
Write a keyset next-page query over a total order (`created_at DESC, id DESC`) with a row-value comparison, and expand it into the equivalent OR form.
Choose the composite index that serves the query, matching column order and sort direction, including extra equality filters.
Fetch the previous page by flipping the comparison and the order, and design an opaque cursor with `has_more` via `LIMIT n + 1`.
Argue when OFFSET is acceptable and what to show instead of an exact total count.

concepts.title: OFFSET reads what it skips
concepts.body: `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40` does not jump to row 41: Postgres produces rows in order and **throws away** the first 40, so page k with page size 20 reads 20k rows (index entries plus heap fetches) to return 20. Page 1 is cheap, page 500 reads 10,000 rows, and a crawler that walks every page does quadratic total work. The plan below is real PGlite output on 5,000 posts with an index on `(created_at DESC, id DESC)`: the index scan emitted 2,020 rows for a 20-row page. The index removes the sort, not the skipping. OFFSET also has no memory: it counts positions in the current data, which leads to drift (next concept).
concepts.code:
-- Page 101 of 20 posts per page
SELECT id FROM posts
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 2000;

-- EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, BUFFERS OFF):
-- Limit (actual rows=20.00 loops=1)
--   ->  Index Only Scan using posts_feed_idx on posts (actual rows=2020.00 loops=1)
--         Heap Fetches: 2020

concepts.title: Pages drift when rows move
concepts.body: OFFSET names a **position**, and writes move rows between positions. If a post is published after the client read page 1, every older post shifts down one place and page 2 starts with the last post of page 1: a **duplicate**. If a post on page 1 is deleted, rows shift up and the first post that belonged on page 2 is never shown: a **gap**. With a feed that gets many writes per second, deep pages drift constantly. Repeatable-read transactions do not help because each page is a separate request. The fix is to remember the last row the client saw and continue strictly after it, which is keyset pagination.
concepts.code:
-- Page 1 showed posts 50..31. Post 51 is inserted. Page 2:
SELECT id FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20;
-- starts at post 31 again (duplicate)

-- Keyset page 2 continues after post 31, whatever was inserted above it:
SELECT id FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2025-03-01 09:31:00+00', 31)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;

concepts.title: Keyset: seek past the last row, over a total order
concepts.body: Keyset (seek) pagination replaces "skip N rows" with "rows that sort after the last one I returned": `WHERE (created_at, id) < ($last_created_at, $last_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20`. The `ORDER BY` must be a **total order**, which means ending in a unique column. `created_at` alone is not unique: two posts in the same microsecond (or a bulk import with one timestamp) are tied, and a cursor of only `created_at` either drops the unseen tied rows (`<`) or repeats the seen ones (`<=`). Adding the primary key as a tie-breaker gives each row exactly one position, so "after this row" is well defined. Make the sort columns `NOT NULL` (as here): a NULL in a row comparison yields NULL and the row silently disappears from every page. Cost is O(log n + page size) at any depth.
concepts.code:
-- Next page, newest first; $1, $2 come from the cursor (last row of the previous page)
SELECT id, author, created_at
FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- First page: the same query without the WHERE clause.

concepts.title: The row-value comparison and its OR form
concepts.body: `(a, b) < (x, y)` is a standard SQL row-constructor comparison, and Postgres evaluates it lexicographically: it is exactly `a < x OR (a = x AND b < y)`. Both return the same rows, but they plan differently. The row form becomes one B-tree `Index Cond`, a single seek. The OR form, in our PGlite test, became a `Filter` on an index scan that started at the newest row: "Rows Removed by Filter: 3201" to return 20. Adding the redundant bound `a <= x AND (a < x OR b < y)` restores an index condition on `a`. You need the OR form when sort directions are **mixed** (`priority DESC, created_at ASC`): a row comparison applies one operator to every column, so expand it by hand, `priority < $p OR (priority = $p AND created_at > $t) OR (...)`.
concepts.code:
-- Equivalent predicates for ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC:
WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2)                        -- Index Cond: ROW(created_at, id) < ROW(...)
WHERE created_at < $1 OR (created_at = $1 AND id < $2)    -- Filter (scans from the top)
WHERE created_at <= $1 AND (created_at < $1 OR id < $2)   -- Index Cond on created_at + Filter

-- Mixed directions cannot use one row comparison:
-- ORDER BY priority DESC, created_at ASC, id ASC
WHERE priority < $p
   OR (priority = $p AND (created_at, id) > ($t, $id))

concepts.title: The index that serves it
concepts.body: Keyset pagination is fast only if an index returns rows in exactly the query's order, so Postgres can seek to the cursor and stop after `LIMIT` rows. For `ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC` use an index on `(created_at DESC, id DESC)`; `(created_at, id)` works too, because a B-tree can be scanned backward (`Index Scan Backward`). What fails is a **mixed** direction such as `(created_at DESC, id)`: in PGlite it used the index for `created_at` and added an `Incremental Sort` for `id`. Put **equality** filter columns first: a per-author feed `WHERE author_id = $a AND (created_at, id) < (...)` wants `(author_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)`. A permanent filter such as `NOT hidden` fits a partial index. Add `INCLUDE (...)` columns if you want index-only scans.

concepts.title: Previous page: flip, then reverse
concepts.body: To go back, the cursor is the **first** row of the current page, and you want the rows just before it in feed order, which are the newer ones. Flip the comparison (`<` becomes `>`) and flip the order (`DESC` becomes `ASC`) so the rows **nearest** the cursor come first and `LIMIT` keeps those. Then reverse them to show newest first, in the API or with an outer `ORDER BY`. The common bug is flipping only the comparison: `(created_at, id) > cursor ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20` returns the 20 newest posts in the whole table, not the page before. The same index serves both directions.
concepts.code:
WITH prev AS (
  SELECT id, author, created_at
  FROM posts
  WHERE (created_at, id) > ($first_created_at, $first_id)
  ORDER BY created_at, id          -- nearest newer rows first
  LIMIT 20
)
SELECT * FROM prev
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC; -- back to feed order

concepts.title: Counts, has_more, and when OFFSET is fine
concepts.body: An exact total is expensive in Postgres: there is no stored row count (MVCC means each transaction may see a different number), so `count(*)` scans the table or a whole index, every time. `count(*) OVER ()` on a paged query is worse than it looks: the window runs before `LIMIT`, so it counts every matching row. Usually the UI only needs **has_more**: fetch `LIMIT n + 1` and check whether the extra row came back. For a number, use an estimate (`pg_class.reltuples` for a table, the planner's row estimate from `EXPLAIN` for a filter), or a capped count (`SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT 1 ... LIMIT 1001) s` shown as "1000+"). OFFSET is fine for small or bounded results (an admin table of a few thousand rows, search results capped at 10 pages), or when users really need "jump to page N", which keyset cannot do.
concepts.code:
-- has_more without counting: ask for one extra row
SELECT id, created_at FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 21;                                  -- 21 rows back => has_more, show 20

-- Cheap estimate of the table size (updated by VACUUM / ANALYZE)
SELECT reltuples::bigint AS approx_rows FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'posts';

-- Capped count: "1000+"
SELECT count(*) AS n FROM (SELECT 1 FROM posts WHERE author_id = $1 LIMIT 1001) s;

walkthrough.title: Designing a feed endpoint, aloud
walkthrough.body: Start with the order: "newest first, `created_at DESC`, and `id DESC` as the tie-breaker because timestamps collide". Then the query: keyset with a row comparison, page size + 1. Then the index: `(created_at DESC, id DESC)`, so each page is a seek plus 21 index entries at any depth. Then the contract: the response has `items`, `next_cursor` and `has_more`; the cursor is opaque (base64 of `{"t": "2025-03-01 09:05:00.123456+00", "id": 4, "v": 1}`, optionally signed) so clients cannot edit it and you can change its format later. Encode the timestamp at **full precision**: JavaScript `Date` keeps milliseconds while `timestamptz` stores microseconds, and a truncated cursor sorts before the real row, so the client sees it again. Finally say what you give up: no page numbers and no exact total.
walkthrough.code:
-- $1, $2 decoded from the cursor; first page omits the WHERE clause
SELECT id, author, created_at
FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1::timestamptz, $2::bigint)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 21;
-- API: has_more = rows.length > 20; items = rows[0..19];
--      next_cursor = has_more ? encode(items[19].created_at::text, items[19].id) : null

walkthrough.title: Keyset with a filter
walkthrough.body: Filters are just extra `WHERE` conditions; the cursor still holds only the sort key. Two rules make it correct and fast. First, the filter must be part of the cursor's identity: if the client changes the filter, start from page 1 (store a hash of the filter in the cursor and reject a mismatch), because the old cursor's position means nothing in the new result. Second, the index must lead with the **equality** columns and then the sort key, so the seek lands inside that author's slice of the index. A range filter (`created_at >= now() - interval '7 days'`) on the sort column itself is fine; a range filter on a different column cannot narrow the seek and becomes a filter that may read many rows to fill a page, so measure it.
walkthrough.code:
-- Feed of one author's visible posts, page after the cursor
SELECT id, created_at
FROM posts
WHERE author_id = $1
  AND NOT hidden
  AND (created_at, id) < ($2, $3)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 21;

CREATE INDEX posts_author_visible_idx
  ON posts (author_id, created_at DESC, id DESC) WHERE NOT hidden;

example:
-- Next page of an author's feed, newest first, with has_more and a cursor for the following page.
WITH probe AS (
  SELECT id, author_id, body, created_at
  FROM posts
  WHERE author_id = 42
    AND (created_at, id) < (timestamptz '2025-03-01 09:05:00.123456+00', 9184)
  ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
  LIMIT 21
), page AS (
  SELECT *, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) AS pos
  FROM probe
)
SELECT id, body, created_at,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM probe) > 20                    AS has_more,
       CASE WHEN pos = 20 THEN created_at::text || '|' || id END AS next_cursor_raw
FROM page
WHERE pos <= 20
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC;
task: Tables `posts(id, author, body, created_at)` and `page_cursor(created_at, id)`. The feed shows posts newest first: by `created_at` descending, and by `id` descending when timestamps are equal. `created_at` is `NOT NULL`, and several posts can share a timestamp. `page_cursor` holds exactly one row: the `created_at` and `id` of the **last** post of the page the client already has. Return the **next page**: the 3 posts that come right after the cursor in feed order (fewer if the feed ends; none if the cursor is the last post). Return `id`, `author`, `created_at`, sorted in feed order (`created_at` descending, then `id` descending). The cursor's post may have been deleted since; continue from its position anyway. Do not use OFFSET.
starter:
-- Next page after the cursor: id, author, created_at; newest first; 3 rows.
SELECT p.id, p.author, p.created_at
FROM posts p, page_cursor c
WHERE p.created_at < c.created_at
ORDER BY p.created_at DESC
LIMIT 3;
hints: If the cursor is at 09:05 and two more posts share 09:05 with smaller ids, `created_at < cursor` skips them. What must you compare when the timestamps are equal?
`(p.created_at, p.id) < (c.created_at, c.id)` compares the timestamps first and the ids only on a tie. Order by both columns descending so the order is total, and `LIMIT 3`.
solution:
A keyset page is "rows strictly after the cursor in a total order". The order is `created_at DESC, id DESC`; the `id` makes it total, because timestamps tie. "After" in a descending order means "smaller", and on the pair: `(p.created_at, p.id) < (c.created_at, c.id)`, which Postgres evaluates as `created_at < x OR (created_at = x AND id < y)`. That keeps older posts and, inside the cursor's tie group, only the ones with a smaller id, which are the unseen ones. The cursor row itself is excluded, so nothing repeats. The starter compares `created_at` only, so it skips every unseen post that shares the cursor's timestamp, and its `ORDER BY` has no tie-breaker, so tied rows come back in any order. A deleted cursor row does not matter: the comparison uses its values, not its existence. The cross join with the one-row `page_cursor` stands in for bind parameters. With an index on `(created_at DESC, id DESC)` this is one index seek plus 3 entries, at any page depth.

```sql
SELECT p.id, p.author, p.created_at
FROM posts p
CROSS JOIN page_cursor c
WHERE (p.created_at, p.id) < (c.created_at, c.id)
ORDER BY p.created_at DESC, p.id DESC
LIMIT 3;
```
checklist: Posts that share the cursor's `created_at` but have a smaller `id` are on the next page; the cursor post is not.
The `ORDER BY` ends with the unique `id`, in the same direction as the comparison.
Post ids that are not in time order (a backfilled import) are still paged by time.
A cursor whose post was deleted still works, and a cursor on the last post returns no rows.
Output columns are exactly `id`, `author`, `created_at`, in feed order, and there is no OFFSET.
pitfalls: A cursor of only `created_at`: `<` drops unseen rows that tie with the cursor, `<=` repeats the rows already shown.
Comparing the columns separately (`created_at <= $1 AND id < $2`): it drops older posts that happen to have larger ids. Use the row comparison or the full OR form.
An `ORDER BY` without a unique tie-breaker: tied rows may come back in a different order on each request, so pages overlap or skip.
A previous-page query that flips the comparison but keeps `DESC`: it returns the newest rows in the table, not the page before.
An index whose directions do not match the query (`created_at DESC, id ASC` for `ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC`): it adds a sort step on every page.
Encoding the cursor timestamp through a millisecond type (JavaScript `Date`): the truncated value sorts before the real row, so rows repeat.
Nullable sort columns: a NULL makes the row comparison NULL, so the row is on no page. Use `NOT NULL` columns or `coalesce` in both the index and the query.
`count(*) OVER ()` on a paged query to show a total: the window runs before `LIMIT` and counts every matching row.

extraPractice.title: First page with has_more
extraPractice.prompt: Table `articles(id, title, published_at)`, `published_at NOT NULL`. Return the **first page** of the newest 3 articles, ordered by `published_at` descending and then `id` descending, with a boolean `has_more` on every row: true when at least one more article exists after this page. Return `id`, `title`, `published_at`, `has_more` in that order and sort. Do not count the whole table: read at most one extra row.
hints: Fetch one more row than the page size. If 4 rows come back, there is a next page.
Put the `LIMIT 4` query in a CTE; select from it with `LIMIT 3` and compare `(SELECT count(*) FROM probe) > 3`.
extraPractice.solution:
WITH probe AS (
  SELECT id, title, published_at
  FROM articles
  ORDER BY published_at DESC, id DESC
  LIMIT 4                      -- page size + 1
)
SELECT id, title, published_at,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM probe) > 3 AS has_more
FROM probe
ORDER BY published_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 3;
checklist: Exactly 3 articles means `has_more` is false; exactly 4 means true.
Ties on `published_at` are ordered by `id` descending, so the page edge is well defined.
The query never reads more than 4 rows from the index.

extraPractice.title: Previous page of a filtered feed
extraPractice.prompt: Tables `posts(id, author, body, created_at, hidden)` and `page_cursor(created_at, id)`; `created_at` is `NOT NULL`. The feed shows visible posts (`hidden` is false) newest first, by `created_at` descending then `id` descending. `page_cursor` holds the **first** (newest) post of the page the client is looking at. Return the **previous page**: the up to 3 visible posts that come immediately **before** the cursor in feed order (the nearest newer posts), returned in feed order (newest first). Return `id`, `author`, `created_at`. Hidden posts are never returned and never count toward the 3.
hints: The rows you want are newer than the cursor, `(created_at, id) > (...)`, but the nearest ones. Which order puts the nearest newer rows first?
Order ascending and `LIMIT 3` in a CTE, filter `NOT hidden` there too, then sort the CTE's rows descending in the outer query.
extraPractice.solution:
WITH prev AS (
  SELECT p.id, p.author, p.created_at
  FROM posts p
  CROSS JOIN page_cursor c
  WHERE NOT p.hidden
    AND (p.created_at, p.id) > (c.created_at, c.id)
  ORDER BY p.created_at, p.id          -- walk towards newer posts, nearest first
  LIMIT 3
)
SELECT id, author, created_at
FROM prev
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC;     -- flip back to feed order
checklist: With more than 3 newer posts, the 3 nearest the cursor are returned, not the 3 newest overall.
Hidden posts are skipped and the next visible post takes their place.
Ties around the cursor are resolved by `id`, and the result is in feed order.

followUps.question: Product wants "jump to page 37" on a table of 50 million rows. What do you say?
followUps.answer: Keyset cannot jump; it can only continue from a row. Options: cap deep paging (search engines stop at about 10 pages) and keep OFFSET for those few pages; replace page numbers with a jump by value ("posts from March 2025" is a seek on `created_at`); or precompute bookmarks every 1,000 rows in a side table refreshed periodically and seek from the nearest one. Whatever you choose, an unbounded `OFFSET 740000` means reading 740,000 rows per request, and the drift remains.

followUps.question: The feed sorts by `score DESC`, and scores change while users scroll. How does keyset behave?
followUps.answer: The cursor holds `(score, id)` of the last row shown. If a row's score changes, it moves to another place in the order: a row that rises above the cursor is never shown, and a row that falls below it is shown twice. Keyset still never reads extra rows, but it cannot fix a moving order. Options: sort on an immutable value (creation time, or a score frozen when the ranking is computed), page through a snapshot of the ranking stored with a version id that goes in the cursor, or accept it and de-duplicate ids on the client.

followUps.question: Why is `count(*)` slow in Postgres, and what do you show instead of "1,234,567 results"?
followUps.answer: MVCC: whether a row is visible depends on the reader's snapshot, so Postgres keeps no row counter. `count(*)` must scan the table or an index (an index-only scan is cheaper only if the visibility map is mostly set). Show `has_more` from `LIMIT n + 1`; an estimate from `pg_class.reltuples` or from `EXPLAIN`'s row estimate for a filtered query ("about 1.2M"); or a capped count read with `LIMIT 1001` ("1000+"). If an exact count is a product requirement, maintain it in a counter table updated by triggers or in batches, and be aware that a single hot counter row becomes a point of lock contention.

followUps.question: How do you paginate `ORDER BY priority DESC, created_at ASC`?
followUps.answer: A row comparison applies one operator to all columns, so it only fits when every column goes the same way. Expand it by hand: `priority < $p OR (priority = $p AND (created_at, id) > ($t, $id))`, with the tie-breaker going the same way as the column before it. Index `(priority DESC, created_at ASC, id ASC)` to match. Add the redundant `priority <= $p` so the planner gets an index condition rather than a filter. For a numeric column you can also index an expression such as `(-priority, created_at, id)` and use a single row comparison on it.

followUps.question: Your cursor is base64 JSON. What can go wrong, and how do you harden it?
followUps.answer: Clients decode and edit it, so validate the types and reject unknown versions. If it contains anything sensitive (a filter on a tenant, a private sort key), sign it with an HMAC or encrypt it. Include the filter and sort so a cursor from one query is rejected on another. Keep timestamp precision (store the text form of `timestamptz`, not a millisecond epoch). Expect a cursor whose row was deleted, and treat it as a position, not as a row lookup. Give cursors no expiry semantics unless you page through snapshots.

takeaways: OFFSET reads and discards every skipped row: page k of size n reads about n·k rows.
OFFSET counts positions, so inserts and deletes between requests cause duplicates and gaps; a keyset cursor names a row.
Keyset needs a total order: end the `ORDER BY` with a unique column and put it in the cursor.
`(a, b) < (x, y)` means `a < x OR (a = x AND b < y)`; the row form plans as one index seek, the OR form may not.
Index the equality filters first, then the sort columns in the query's order and directions.
Previous page: flip `<` to `>` and `DESC` to `ASC`, `LIMIT`, then reverse. `has_more` comes from `LIMIT n + 1`, not from a count.

diagrams.title: Index entries read to serve one page of 20
diagrams.alt: Bar chart of index entries read per page with a page size of 20. OFFSET page 1 reads 20, page 50 reads 1,000, page 100 reads 2,000 and page 500 reads 10,000, because page k reads 20 times k entries. A keyset query for page 500 reads only 20, the same as page 1.
diagrams.caption: OFFSET page k reads 20k entries and throws away 20(k−1) of them; keyset reads one page's worth at any depth.

diagrams.title: Page drift: a new post arrives between page 1 and page 2
diagrams.alt: Timeline of a feed paginated with LIMIT 20 OFFSET. The client reads page 1, posts 50 down to 31. Post 51 is then inserted, shifting every post down one position. Page 2 with OFFSET 20 now starts at post 31, so post 31 is shown twice. A keyset request for rows after post 31 returns posts 30 to 11 and is unaffected.
diagrams.caption: OFFSET counts positions, and writes move rows between positions; a keyset cursor names a row, so inserts and deletes elsewhere cannot shift it.

events.label: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 0 returns posts 50 down to 31.
Post 51 is published: every older post moves down one position.
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20 skips posts 51–32 and starts at post 31.
Post 31 is shown twice. A delete instead would have shifted rows up and skipped one.
Page 2 asks for rows after (created_at, id) of post 31: posts 30 down to 11.
Post 51 appears when the client reloads the first page.

diagrams.title: Page 3 of 20: OFFSET walks, keyset seeks
diagrams.alt: Comparison of fetching the third page of 20 posts. On the left, LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40 starts at the newest index entry, reads 60 entries, discards the first 40 and returns 20. On the right, the cursor (created_at, id) of the last post on page 2 is used as a search key: the B-tree descends straight to it, reads the next 20 entries and returns all of them.
diagrams.caption: OFFSET cost grows with page depth because skipped rows are still read; a keyset query descends the index to the cursor and reads only the rows it returns.

diagrams.title: How (created_at, id) < (x, y) decides a row
diagrams.alt: Flow diagram of a row-value comparison. A post's pair (a, b) is compared with the cursor (x, y). First a is compared with x: if a is less than x the post is older and kept; if a is greater it is newer and dropped. Only when a equals x is the tie broken by comparing b with y: b less than y keeps the post, otherwise it is dropped, which also drops the cursor row itself.
diagrams.caption: The row comparison is lexicographic: it equals a < x OR (a = x AND b < y). The second column only matters inside a tie, so it must be unique.

steps.text: Each candidate post's `(created_at, id)` is compared with the cursor `(x, y)` taken from the last row of the previous page.
The first columns decide unless they are equal: an older timestamp is kept, a newer one dropped. The ids are never looked at.
Equal timestamps are a tie. This is the case a `created_at < x` cursor gets wrong: it drops every tied post the client has not seen yet.
Inside the tie the unique `id` decides. `id < y` keeps the unseen tied posts; `id = y` is the cursor row itself and is excluded, so nothing repeats.

diagrams.title: One round trip of a cursor-paginated feed API
diagrams.alt: Flow diagram of a feed API. The client sends GET /feed with an opaque cursor. The API decodes it into created_at and id and runs a keyset query with LIMIT 21. Postgres returns up to 21 rows. The API keeps 20, sets has_more if a 21st row came back, and encodes the last kept row's created_at and id as next_cursor. The response with items and next_cursor goes back to the client, which sends it on the next request.
diagrams.caption: The cursor is the last row's sort key, made opaque; LIMIT n + 1 answers has_more without counting.

steps.text: The client sends back the cursor exactly as it received it. It is opaque (for example base64 of a small JSON with the sort key, the filter and a version), so clients cannot build or edit one.
The API decodes and validates the cursor (reject it if the filter or sort changed) and runs the keyset query with page size + 1 as the limit.
Postgres seeks to the cursor in the `(created_at DESC, id DESC)` index and reads at most 21 entries. If 21 come back, there is a next page.
The API drops the 21st row, takes the last kept row's `created_at` and `id` (at full microsecond precision) and encodes them as `next_cursor`, or null when `has_more` is false.
The client stores `next_cursor` and sends it for the next page. No page numbers and no total count are needed.

diagrams.title: Previous page: flip the comparison and the order, then reverse
diagrams.alt: Sequence diagram with a client, an API and Postgres. The client asks for the page before a cursor that holds the first row it is showing. The API queries Postgres for rows greater than the cursor ordered ascending with a limit, so the rows nearest the cursor come first. Postgres returns them oldest first; the API reverses them to newest first before replying with the page and both cursors.
diagrams.caption: Going backwards uses the same index scanned the other way; reverse the rows afterwards so every page is shown in feed order.

messages.label: (t, id) > (x, y) ORDER BY t, id
messages.note: Comparison flipped from < to >, order flipped from DESC to ASC, LIMIT n + 1.

messages.label: rows reversed: newest first
messages.note: Reverse in the API or with an outer ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC.

messages.label: GET /feed?after=<last row>
messages.note: Forward paging continues from the last row shown, as before.

exercises.starter:
-- Next page after the cursor: id, author, created_at; newest first; 3 rows.
SELECT p.id, p.author, p.created_at
FROM posts p, page_cursor c
WHERE p.created_at < c.created_at
ORDER BY p.created_at DESC
LIMIT 3;
exercises.solution:
SELECT p.id, p.author, p.created_at
FROM posts p
CROSS JOIN page_cursor c
WHERE (p.created_at, p.id) < (c.created_at, c.id)
ORDER BY p.created_at DESC, p.id DESC
LIMIT 3;

exercises.starter:
-- First page (3 newest) plus has_more: id, title, published_at, has_more.
WITH page AS (
  SELECT id, title, published_at
  FROM articles
  ORDER BY published_at DESC
  LIMIT 3
)
SELECT id, title, published_at,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM page) > 3 AS has_more
FROM page
ORDER BY published_at DESC;
exercises.solution:
WITH probe AS (
  SELECT id, title, published_at
  FROM articles
  ORDER BY published_at DESC, id DESC
  LIMIT 4                      -- page size + 1
)
SELECT id, title, published_at,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM probe) > 3 AS has_more
FROM probe
ORDER BY published_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 3;

exercises.starter:
-- Previous page: the 3 visible posts just newer than the cursor, returned newest first.
SELECT p.id, p.author, p.created_at
FROM posts p, page_cursor c
WHERE (p.created_at, p.id) > (c.created_at, c.id)
ORDER BY p.created_at DESC, p.id DESC
LIMIT 3;
exercises.solution:
WITH prev AS (
  SELECT p.id, p.author, p.created_at
  FROM posts p
  CROSS JOIN page_cursor c
  WHERE NOT p.hidden
    AND (p.created_at, p.id) > (c.created_at, c.id)
  ORDER BY p.created_at, p.id          -- walk towards newer posts, nearest first
  LIMIT 3
)
SELECT id, author, created_at
FROM prev
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC;     -- flip back to feed order

predict.explain: Row comparison is lexicographic. `(2, 5) < (2, 7)`: tie on 2, then 5 < 7. `(1, 9) < (2, 0)`: 1 < 2 decides, the 9 is never compared. `(3, 0) < (2, 9)`: 3 > 2 decides. It is not a column-by-column AND, which would make `b` false.

predict.code:
-- Feed order: ts DESC, id DESC. Page 1 showed ids 3, 2; the cursor stored only ts = 10.
WITH feed(id, ts) AS (VALUES (1, 10), (2, 10), (3, 10), (4, 9))
SELECT id FROM feed
WHERE ts < 10
ORDER BY ts DESC, id DESC
predict.explain: Post 1 shares the cursor's timestamp but was not shown yet; `ts < 10` drops it forever. The cursor needs the tie-breaker: `(ts, id) < (10, 2)` returns 1, then 4.

predict.code:
-- Page 1 (LIMIT 2 OFFSET 0) showed 6, 5. Then post 7 is inserted. Page 2:
WITH feed(id) AS (VALUES (7), (6), (5), (4), (3), (2), (1))
SELECT id FROM feed ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2
predict.explain: OFFSET 2 now skips 7 and 6, so page 2 starts with 5, which page 1 already showed. A keyset query `WHERE id < 5` would return 4, 3 regardless of the insert.

predict.code: SELECT (1, NULL::int) < (2, 0) AS a, (1, NULL::int) < (1, 5) AS b
predict.explain: The first pair decides `a` (1 < 2), so the NULL is never compared. In `b` the first columns tie and the comparison reaches `NULL < 5`, which is NULL, so a row like that would be on no page. Keep sort columns `NOT NULL`.

predict.code:
SELECT id, count(*) OVER () AS total
FROM generate_series(1, 10) AS id
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 2
predict.explain: Window functions run before `LIMIT`, so `count(*) OVER ()` counts every row the query matched. It gives a total, but it costs a full read of the result even for one page. Use `LIMIT n + 1` for `has_more`, or an estimate.

lab.tip: Before writing the query, say the order out loud and prove it is total: "newest first, `created_at DESC`, then `id DESC` because timestamps tie". Then say the cursor is the last row's `(created_at, id)`, write the row comparison, and name the index `(created_at DESC, id DESC)`. Interviewers listen for three things: the tie-breaker, why OFFSET is O(depth) and drifts, and `LIMIT n + 1` instead of a count.
